scope.configuration: Specialist gangs assigned to Rome's conduits and distribution.

linked_claims.statement: Frontinus reports about 240 publicly owned and 460 imperial enslaved aqueduct workers organised into specialised maintenance functions.

test.reason: Attribution to a specific ancient account, with performance limits explicit.

linked_claims.inference_limits: High confidence in the reported arrangement, not an independently verified staffing census.

linked_claims.statement: Frontinus describes recurrent funding and timed, sequential shutdowns as arrangements for maintaining Rome's aqueduct service.

test.mechanism_chain: Funding and advance scheduling -> personnel/materials available during limited shutdowns -> intended preservation of supply.
test.strongest_rival: Actual reliability may have depended more on redundant routes and favourable water sources, with rules poorly observed.
test.discriminating_observation: Work records or dated repairs showing compliance and service changes before/after procedural changes.
test.evidence_sought_found: ANC-S05 prescriptive and financial passages inspected; no independent operational audit found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Administrative intention cannot be equated with realised performance.

linked_claims.inference_limits: No causal estimate of improved reliability or fiscal adequacy.

edge_record.qualification: Physical dependence inside the reported boatmill configuration.

scope.configuration: Wheels suspended between moored boats are driven by current.

alternatives: Different power sources could supply milling with a different configuration.
edge_record.necessity_rationale: Without current through these wheels, their reported motive input disappears.
edge_record.dispute: Exact current velocities and hull/wheel design are unspecified.

linked_claims.statement: Procopius reports aqueduct disruption stopping Rome's mills in 537, fodder scarcity limiting animal substitution, and Tiber boatmills restoring grinding while wells still supplied drinking water.

test.mechanism_chain: Siege cuts aqueduct flow and limits fodder -> existing mills and animal alternatives are constrained -> river-driven boatmills substitute for grinding.
test.strongest_rival: Some milling may have continued elsewhere; the emergency innovation may be less comprehensive than the narrative claims.
test.discriminating_observation: Contemporary grain/mill records and securely dated traces of competing installations during the siege.
test.evidence_sought_found: ANC-S07 explicitly links disruption, feed scarcity and boatmills; drinking water has other sources.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Detailed sequence is one literary witness and cannot quantify city-wide adequacy.

linked_claims.inference_limits: No throughput, household coverage or proof of permanent aqueduct abandonment.

edges.selection: Ordinary noncontroversial physical relation; necessity direction control.
edges.assessment: Procopius Wars V.19.20–22 describes wheels between moored boats driven by current. depends-on points from boatmill to current, correctly. High physical confidence need not equal confidence in the narrative’s city-wide sufficiency. Removing current disables this configuration; different power substitutes change the configuration. No diffusion denominator claimed.

edge_record.qualification: Hydraulic configurations only; mine pumping also used human and animal power. No universal water prerequisite.

scope.configuration: Direct/remote mine drainage under site-specific water and transmission conditions; Hydraulic configurations only; mine pumping also used human and animal power. No universal water prerequisite.

edge_record.dispute: Hydraulic configurations only; mine pumping also used human and animal power. No universal water prerequisite.

linked_claims.statement: Agricola’s 1556 account presents human, animal and hydraulic mine-work choices together and includes repairable components and site access among practical considerations.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

linked_claims.inference_limits: Supports existence of described techniques and stated criteria, not measured prevalence, profitability or a universal choice rule.

linked_claims.statement: In sixteenth- and seventeenth-century central European mining, rod transmission extended the use of waterpower to pumps distant from the stream; non-steam engineering continued to change.

test.mechanism_chain: Remote hydraulic resource -> construct rod linkage -> mechanical power reaches distant pumps -> expanded site choice.
test.strongest_rival: Static post-Agricola mining would predict little relevant configuration change; a weaker rival accepts change but denies cost advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Later mechanisms and installations absent from Agricola distinguish change; operating accounts are needed for cost advantage.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Agricola and Multhauf (IND-S01/S02); latter compares remote rod/ balanced transmission and later depictions.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Configuration change is supported; diffusion rate and net advantage remain unresolved.

linked_claims.inference_limits: No region-wide diffusion denominator. Adequate hydraulics delaying German steam adoption is a further hypothesis, not established by this claim.

edges.selection: Endpoint of cross-case shared-node path; technical possibility versus operation.
edges.assessment: The edge itself is scoped to central-European mine drainage and uses technical-possibility rather than claiming prevalence. IND-K01 is appropriately descriptive about Agricola; IND-K02 supports configuration change, not cost advantage. IND-T02 nevertheless shares identity with British textile waterpower in IND-C03. Scope text does not satisfy the v2 separate-local-nodes requirement.

edge_record.qualification: Steam and usable water were alternative power sources at particular mill locations; national potential is not the choice denominator.

scope.configuration: British textile-mill power choices, including unrealised collective reservoirs; Steam and usable water were alternative power sources at particular mill locations; national potential is not the choice denominator.

edge_record.dispute: Steam and usable water were alternative power sources at particular mill locations; national potential is not the choice denominator.

linked_claims.statement: Jonell and colleagues reconstruct unused waterpower potential across much of Britain alongside local constraints around Greater Manchester, and describe supplementary steam use in water-powered mills.

test.mechanism_chain: Local dependable water constraints -> mill seeks extra power -> steam supplement/replacement -> capacity expansion.
test.strongest_rival: Labour access/control or agglomeration could favour steam despite adequate water; national abundance predicts no shortage only if local access is ignored.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable mills/sites with usable flow versus scarce flow, plus seasonal output and expansion decisions.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S05 impact/method sections: local Manchester constraint alongside national potential and supplementary steam; compared IND-S06 coordination abstract.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Industrial clustering partly creates scarcity; reservoir costs, rights and labour conditions unresolved.

linked_claims.inference_limits: Partial-text inspection only; underlying model and supplements not rerun. Local scarcity does not identify why factories originally clustered there.

linked_claims.statement: Malm argues that large proposed reservoir schemes in the 1820s–1830s failed partly because their collective financing and coordination requirements conflicted with manufacturers’ arrangements.

test.mechanism_chain: Shared reservoir requires funding and allocation -> manufacturers cannot coordinate -> proposed expansion not built.
test.strongest_rival: Projects may be physically unreliable or financially unattractive even under feasible collective governance.
test.discriminating_observation: Scheme correspondence and cost/flow evidence showing viable projects blocked specifically by coordination, compared with realised schemes.
test.evidence_sought_found: Searched full article; only IND-S06 author abstract acquired. It explicitly makes the coordination claim; scheme-level evidence not found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Both rivals fit non-building. Weak-access claim retained only as attributed hypothesis.

linked_claims.inference_limits: Abstract-only evidence: claim is about the author’s interpretation, not an independent finding that water was consistently cheaper or every proposed scheme feasible.

edges.assessment: The reciprocal joint-input reference to IND-T30 is consistent with IND-E27. Onsite generation is named as an alternative, and the claim is undetermined rather than identified. edge_record.qualification: Meroe experiments establish process-specific ore sensitivity; does not imply every listed ore is usable.

scope.configuration: Production of new iron by ore reduction in the reported Meroe replica experiments

alternatives: Other suitable iron ores may substitute
Imported metal bypasses the primary-reduction task
edge_record.necessity_rationale: Within primary ore-reduction production of new iron, removing all iron-bearing feedstock prevents that output. This does not require a specific ore deposit, local ownership, or primary smelting rather than buying metal.
edge_record.dispute: Oolitic ore was promising; not every ore source or mixture was tested.

linked_claims.statement: Meroe replica smelts improved after changes in ore, air delivery and operation, demonstrating coupled operating constraints rather than the sufficiency of a copied furnace shape.

test.mechanism_chain: Suitable ore plus adjusted blast/charging and operator coordination -> better reduction/slag behaviour -> more workable products in replica trials.
test.strongest_rival: Different modern operating choices could also succeed; apparent improvement could result from one unisolated variable rather than the whole historical reconstruction.
test.discriminating_observation: Controlled replication changing one parameter at a time, matching archaeological residues and retaining detailed mass balances.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S06 Tables 2–4 and Lessons Learned record failed/low-yield runs and improved combinations; authors flag anecdotal later data.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Joint changes prevent attribution to each input; viability is demonstrated only for tested modern configurations, not a unique ancient procedure.

linked_claims.inference_limits: Modern reconstructed feasibility does not identify the unique ancient process or provide an ancient output series.

edges.selection: Modern experimental necessity sharing a node with ancient deployment.
edges.assessment: The local counterfactual is sound: new iron by ore reduction requires iron-bearing feedstock, while imported metal bypasses the task. MAT-K12 openly acknowledges coupled parameter changes, so evaluated means feasibility evidence rather than isolated effects. MAT-T28 improperly combines ancient later/post-Meroitic process and modern replica; split identities despite the experimental scope text.

edges.selection: Ancient archaeological fuel contribution connected to experimental necessity through MAT-T28.
edges.assessment: MAT-K13 describes archaeological charcoal selection; observed-contribution with alternative taxa and unresolved provenance avoids a claim that acacia is uniquely necessary or sustainable. The ancient edge nevertheless targets a node naming both ancient operation and modern replicas. MAT-E08→MAT-E06 is therefore a cross-subepisode path that must not imply the ancient fuel record proves the replica’s input configuration or vice versa.

edge_record.qualification: Author-summary mechanism; not a universal necessity or independently ranked cause.

scope.configuration: AT&T switching within its early twentieth-century service organisation

edge_record.dispute: Abstract-level mechanism support; competing technical/scale explanations not independently adjudicated.

linked_claims.statement: The AT&T historical study attributes delayed switching automation to organisational interdependencies and market-scale economics, rather than treating invention as immediate deployability.

test.mechanism_chain: Interdependent manual service -> firm/technology adaptation -> viable switching at suitable scale -> staged adoption
test.strongest_rival: Purely technical improvement or wage-cost changes could drive timing without independent organisational causation.
test.discriminating_observation: Internal plans and comparable exchanges with different organisational readiness or market size.
test.evidence_sought_found: LBR-S01 abstract reports archival interpretation; full mechanism evidence was not acquired, so no adjudication claimed.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The contribution cannot rank organisational adaptation versus technical and economic change.

linked_claims.inference_limits: Abstract-level support; relative causal weights not audited.

edges.selection: Weak-access organisational mechanism and alternative technical/scale explanations.
edges.assessment: The author abstract explicitly states firm/technology adaptation and market-scale profitability. The edge flags author-summary support; LBR-K01 test is underdetermined and says full mechanism evidence was not acquired. observed-contribution is defensible only as an attributed historical interpretation, not an independently identified organisational effect. Full-text archival tests remain necessary before strengthening it.

limits: No full MAT/IND source re-audit, no reconstruction of historical datasets, no running statistical models, no visual browser interaction. Record/claim reading and source-passage review are reported separately. No source material or live main collection was changed.
